terms.definition: A full-length collection of songs, usually 8 or more tracks, released as one body of work.
terms.example: "The album has a clear story arc."

terms.definition: Hip-hop that steps outside mainstream sounds or topics, often mixing genres.
terms.example: "The EP is alternative hip-hop with live instruments."

terms.definition: A male breakdancer. The B stands for break or Bronx, depending on the telling.
terms.example: "He's been a b-boy for twenty years."

terms.definition: A female breakdancer.
terms.example: "The b-girl's footwork won the round."

terms.definition: The second song on a record's flip side, historically less promoted. Now used loosely for extra or alternate tracks.
terms.example: "The B-side ended up being the fan favourite."

terms.definition: Lyric-focused hip-hop associated with the underground and with listeners carrying records and notebooks in their bags.
terms.example: "A backpack rap album built on jazz samples."

terms.definition: Lines of a verse. Usually counted in measures of music, with one bar typically holding one line of lyric.
terms.example: "Sixteen bars on the second verse."
terms.southAfricanContext: Ordz takes its name from this world: words, lyrics, bars and wordplay.

terms.definition: A contest where two MCs trade verses aimed at each other, judged by crowd or panel on wit, delivery and originality.
terms.example: "The battle came down to a final round."
terms.southAfricanContext: SA battle scenes have grown through live events and online videos.

terms.definition: The instrumental backing of a track: drums, bass and other musical elements. Also the rhythm itself.
terms.example: "He sent over three beats this morning."

terms.definition: A person who makes beats. Often used for producers who work mainly with drum programming and samples.
terms.example: "She's a beatmaker from Pretoria who sells beats online."

terms.definition: An outdoor community party with DJs, MCs and dancers. Hip-hop was born at parties like these.
terms.example: "The block party closed the street."

terms.definition: A drum-driven hip-hop style built on hard kicks and snares, often with sampled loops. Associated with 1990s New York.
terms.example: "The producer is known for boom bap beats."
terms.southAfricanContext: Boom bap remains an influence on SA backpack and lyrical scenes.

terms.definition: A drum break from a record that DJs looped and extended. The rhythmic core of early hip-hop.
terms.example: "The breakbeat kept the dancers going."

terms.definition: A dance form with floor moves, spins and freezes. Also called breaking. One of the four classic elements.
terms.example: "Breakdancing crews practised in parking lots."
terms.southAfricanContext: Breaking crews were among the first visible hip-hop groups in 1980s SA.

terms.definition: Entry kept from the original brief. The exact meaning needs to be confirmed by the Ordz editorial team before publication.
terms.southAfricanContext: Editorial note: confirm definition. Related SA bodies include CAPASSO (mechanical rights), SAMRO (performance rights) and SAMPRA (needletime).

terms.definition: The repeated section of a song, usually sung or chanted between verses. In hip-hop it is often called the hook.
terms.example: "The chorus returns after every verse."

terms.definition: Rap that focuses on social, political or spiritual themes.
terms.example: "The album is conscious rap about land and identity."
terms.southAfricanContext: Strongly rooted in SA hip-hop's response to apartheid and its legacy.

terms.definition: Searching through records, often in second-hand shops or markets, to find rare samples and breaks.
terms.example: "He found the loop crate digging in Joburg."

terms.definition: A circle of rappers, beatmakers or dancers who take turns performing, usually unrehearsed. The word also names recorded group freestyle videos.
terms.example: "We caught a street cypher outside the venue."
terms.southAfricanContext: Cyphers are a staple of SA campus and open-mic culture and a common way new MCs get noticed.

terms.definition: The vocal performance of a lyric: tone, energy, diction and emphasis. Two rappers can say the same words and sound nothing alike.
terms.example: "The lyrics were simple, but the delivery made them hit."

terms.definition: A verse or song that attacks another artist. Short for disrespect.
terms.example: "The diss track dropped at midnight."

terms.definition: A company that gets recorded music into shops and onto streaming platforms.
terms.example: "The distributor delivered the album to every platform."

terms.definition: A person who plays and manipulates recorded music, traditionally on turntables. One of hip-hop's four original elements.
terms.example: "The DJ kept the crowd moving all night."
terms.southAfricanContext: SA DJs are central to radio, clubs and mixtape culture.

terms.definition: A phrase with two meanings, one of which is usually indirect or cheeky.
terms.example: "The line works as a joke and as a threat."

terms.definition: Digital service provider. A streaming or download platform such as Spotify, Apple Music or YouTube Music.
terms.example: "Most DSPs require a distributor."

terms.definition: The spelled-out form of MC. Often used when stressing the craft over the persona.
terms.example: "He calls himself an emcee, not a rapper."

terms.definition: Extended play. A release shorter than an album, usually 3 to 7 tracks.
terms.example: "A five-track EP is a good way to introduce yourself."

terms.definition: How a rapper's words sit on the beat: rhythm, cadence, rhyme pattern and pacing.
terms.example: "Her flow switches halfway through the verse."

terms.definition: Rapping improvised on the spot, or lyrics written to a beat without a fixed song structure.
terms.example: "He freestyled for five minutes off a single word from the crowd."

terms.definition: A style that describes street life, crime and survival, often in a confrontational voice.
terms.example: "The gangsta rap record split critics."

terms.definition: A period, generally the late 1980s to mid-1990s, regarded as a peak of creativity in American hip-hop.
terms.example: "Golden era albums set the template."

terms.definition: Stylised public art, often with spray paint, including tags, pieces and murals. One of the four classic elements.
terms.example: "The wall was covered in graffiti."
terms.southAfricanContext: SA graffiti has its own styles, languages and political history.

terms.definition: The catchy, repeatable part of a song that listeners remember. Often sung or chanted.
terms.example: "The hook was stuck in my head all week."

terms.definition: A brand or sub-label operating under a larger company, or an independent brand that releases and curates music and media. Ordz describes itself as an imprint.
terms.example: "The imprint curates independent releases."

terms.definition: An artist, label or project that operates without a major label, with its own funding and decisions.
terms.example: "She released the EP independently."

terms.definition: An artist who releases music without a major-label deal and handles or outsources their own business, from recording to marketing.
terms.example: "As an independent artist she controls her release schedule."
terms.southAfricanContext: The independent route is the main path for most SA hip-hop artists today.

terms.definition: International Standard Recording Code. A unique ID assigned to each recording so it can be tracked and paid.
terms.example: "Register an ISRC for every track before release."

terms.definition: Music with a deliberately rough, warm or imperfect sound, often with tape hiss and dusty samples.
terms.example: "The lo-fi beat felt like a late-night tape."

terms.definition: Long play. Originally a vinyl format, now shorthand for a full-length album.
terms.example: "The LP runs 14 tracks."

terms.definition: Music and artists with wide commercial reach through radio, TV, playlists and large labels.
terms.example: "The song crossed over to the mainstream."

terms.definition: The original finished recording of a song. Owners of the master usually control how it is licensed and earn from its use.
terms.example: "She kept ownership of her masters."

terms.definition: Short for master of ceremonies. In hip-hop, the person who raps or rocks the microphone.
terms.example: "She's the best MC in the cypher tonight."
terms.southAfricanContext: Used across SA scenes in English and in local languages, from Cape Flats Afrikaans to isiZulu and Setswana.

terms.definition: The right to reproduce a composition, for example on CDs, downloads or streams.
terms.example: "Mechanical royalties are paid when a song is reproduced."
terms.southAfricanContext: In SA, CAPASSO administers mechanical rights on behalf of its members.

terms.definition: The information attached to a recording: title, artists, writers, ISRC, release date and more. Wrong metadata means missing payments.
terms.example: "Check the metadata before you submit."

terms.definition: A figure of speech that says one thing is another to create meaning without using like or as.
terms.example: "'The city is a hungry mouth' is a metaphor."

terms.definition: A free or low-cost collection of tracks released outside the traditional album cycle, often to build a following.
terms.example: "Her mixtape went round on WhatsApp before it hit streaming."
terms.southAfricanContext: Mixtapes have long been a route for independent SA artists to reach listeners before any label support.

terms.definition: Newer generations of artists and styles that depart from earlier templates.
terms.example: "The new school is mixing trap with kwaito."

terms.definition: The earliest era of hip-hop, from the 1970s to about the mid-1980s, with party-focused songs and simple production.
terms.example: "Old school routines were built around block parties."

terms.definition: A live event where anyone can sign up to perform.
terms.example: "She tested her first verse at an open mic."
terms.southAfricanContext: Open mics are a key discovery space for SA artists outside the major venues.

terms.definition: The right to perform a composition in public, including on radio, TV and in venues. Performance royalties are collected by collecting societies.
terms.example: "Radio play generates performance royalties."
terms.southAfricanContext: In SA, SAMRO administers performance rights for composers, authors and publishers.

terms.definition: The person who shapes how a record sounds, from the beat and arrangement to guiding the performance and final mix.
terms.example: "The producer pushed the vocal to be rawer."

terms.definition: A company that manages the rights to songs or written works. In music, it collects royalties for songwriters. In media, it publishes content.
terms.example: "Her publisher registers the compositions."

terms.definition: Rights tied to the composition, meaning the music and lyrics, as opposed to the recording.
terms.example: "Publishing rights pay writers when songs are played or sold."

terms.definition: A line that lands a twist or joke, usually at the end of a bar.
terms.example: "That punchline made the whole room react."

terms.definition: Rhythmic, rhymed vocal delivery over a beat. One of hip-hop's four classic elements, alongside DJing, breaking and graffiti.
terms.example: "Rap is the voice of the culture."
terms.southAfricanContext: SA rap is performed in many languages, often mixing them within a single verse.

terms.definition: A company that signs, finances, markets and distributes recorded music.
terms.example: "The label funded the video."

terms.definition: A payment to rights holders each time their work is used, sold or streamed.
terms.example: "The royalty statement arrives every quarter."

terms.definition: A piece of an existing recording reused in a new track.
terms.example: "The sample is a two-second horn stab."

terms.definition: The practice of lifting and reworking parts of existing recordings. Sampled material generally needs clearance from the rights holders.
terms.example: "Sampling shaped the sound of boom bap."
terms.southAfricanContext: SA producers sample jazz, mbaqanga, soul and local funk, which ties the music to the country's own archive.

terms.definition: Moving a record back and forth under the needle to create rhythmic sounds.
terms.example: "His scratching ran through the whole hook."

terms.definition: A comparison using like or as.
terms.example: "Fast like a taxi in rush hour."

terms.definition: A lead track released on its own, often ahead of an album or EP.
terms.example: "The single drops Friday."

terms.definition: Listening to music over the internet without owning a file. Revenue is paid per stream, at very small amounts.
terms.example: "Streaming income depends on volume."
terms.southAfricanContext: SA streaming has grown alongside cheaper data and mobile access.

terms.definition: Synchronisation licensing: placing a recording in a film, advert, game or show, usually for a fee.
terms.example: "A sync deal paid for the whole EP."

terms.definition: A graffiti writer's signature name, written quickly.
terms.example: "His tag was on every wall on that street."

terms.definition: A style with rolling hi-hats, heavy 808 bass and often dark or melodic moods. Originated in the American South.
terms.example: "That trap beat has a huge 808."
terms.southAfricanContext: Trap is a major force in the 2010s and 2020s SA scene, performed in local languages.

terms.definition: Treating the turntable as a musical instrument through scratching, beat juggling and manipulation.
terms.example: "Turntablism turns two records into a new composition."

terms.definition: Music and scenes that exist outside mainstream radio, TV and major-label systems, often valued for risk-taking and authenticity.
terms.example: "The underground feeds the culture before the charts notice."
terms.southAfricanContext: Ordz focuses on the independent and underground scene.

terms.definition: A section of a song where the rapper carries the story or argument, usually 16 bars, though length varies.
terms.example: "Her second verse is the best part of the record."

terms.definition: A complex, interlocking graffiti lettering style that can be hard for outsiders to read.
terms.example: "The wildstyle piece covered the whole wall."

terms.definition: Clever use of language: puns, double meanings, rhyme schemes, switching languages. Central to the Ordz name.
terms.example: "Her wordplay works in two languages at once."
terms.southAfricanContext: Code-switching between languages is a rich source of wordplay in SA hip-hop.
